p.location: p.266, pairwise contrast results beneath Table 3
p.quote:
In phase 0, the control group rated bad items
significantly lower than the intervention group, estimated difference = −0.261, 95%
CI = [−0.456, −0.0653], p = .009. Nevertheless, in phase 1 the control group rated bad items
significantly higher than the intervention group, estimated difference = 0.525, 95% CI = [0.328,
0.722], p < .0001, and phase 2, estimated difference = 0.543, 95% CI = [0.349, 0.7362], p < .0001.
The third column in Table 3 shows the model parameters for predictors group by phase on
knowledge application ratings for each good quality item as a dependent variable. There were no
significant differences between groups for the good items in phase 0 or in phase 2, ps > .05; but
in phase 1 the control group rated good items significantly lower than the intervention group,
estimated difference = −0.2589, 95% CI = [−0.448, −0.07], p = .0073. There were no significant
differences between the ratings in each phase in the control group or in the intervention group,
ps > .05.

reported_success.quote:
Our results are in line with those from the
original study (Pérez et al., 2018). Overall, evidence shows that the intervention improved college
students’ sourcing skills in tasks where they explicitly had to use source information to make decisions
and that the effects lasted to the delayed post-test. Moreover, the results from a novel, ecological task,
a final term team essay with no prompts to use reliable sources, suggest that the intervention also had
effects on naturalistic college online inquiry behavior. ... Our preregistered hypotheses were supported by the data: After the intervention, trained students
became specifically more critical of bad quality websites than the control group, even when the latter
initially outperformed them, and this difference persisted to the delayed post-test.
